gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a two-screen extender's 'plug and play, no driver' and its '300 nits' both come with conditions. The Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro runs both screens without software only on a laptop with two DisplayPort-enabled USB-C ports, one cable per screen. Base M1 and M2 MacBooks and the MacBook Neo need Mobile Pixels' free software to extend to both. Its screens reach full brightness only with a power adapter plugged into the Trio. A one-screen attachable or portable monitor runs on one USB-C cable with no driver.
standout_why: Compared against the two cited pages that loaded and the third cited page, which did not. bestusefultips.com (cited) warns 'Do not assume a laptop that can drive one external monitor can automatically drive two' and that DisplayLink 'may require driver installation', but it names no product and gives no numbers. viewsonic.com (cited) states that the VG1457's dual-screen Extend mode is unavailable on macOS because of MST, with only the lower screen active. That covers its own dual portable monitor, not attach-to-laptop extenders, and says nothing about needing external power for rated brightness. Only the menus of bestbuy.ca (cited) loaded; its article text did not, so I can't say what it states. None of these pages names the per-product condition (two DisplayPort USB-C ports, or software on base M1/M2) or the power-adapter condition behind the brightness figure. None puts weight per added screen, or what hangs on the lid, side by side.
decides: This confirms ChatGPT's lean toward a portable monitor and sharpens it. For one added screen, the honest pick is any single screen on one native USB-C cable (a freestanding portable, the kickstand Duex Float 2 Pro, or the lid-mounted Duex Max DS). It works with no driver on a base M1/M2 MacBook too. An extender earns its place only for two added screens, and only after the shopper counts their laptop's DisplayPort-capable USB-C ports. With fewer than two, or on a base M1/M2 MacBook, it needs the maker's software. The Trio 3 Pro also needs its own power adapter in the bag for its rated 300 nits. On weight, the Trio 3 Pro works out to about 0.95 kg per added screen (1.9 kg for two). The ViewSonic VG1457 dual portable is about 0.59 kg per screen and puts nothing on the lid, but it cannot extend to both screens on macOS.

findings.label: Weight (whole unit, two added screens)
findings.value: 1.9 kg (4.13 lb); about 0.95 kg per added screen
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Simon Jary, Macworld, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Macworld: 4.13 lb (1.9 kg); folded 13.4 x 8.8 x 0.9 in, 40.3 in wide unfolded. Per-screen figure is my arithmetic: 1.9 kg / 2 added screens. The laptop either leans into the centre section or is held by four magnets stuck to the lid. Macworld does not say how much of the weight rests on the lid.

findings.label: Video path (when 'no driver' holds)
findings.value: Two USB-C cables, one per screen; no driver only with two DisplayPort-enabled USB-C ports; base M1/M2 MacBooks and the MacBook Neo need Mobile Pixels' free software
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Simon Jary, Macworld, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Macworld quotes the manual: with 'two DP enabled USB-C ports' driver installation 'is not necessary'. Macworld says base M1/M2 Macs and the MacBook Neo drive one external monitor without the software, and compares the software to DisplayLink. It says M1/M2/M3 Pro/Max and any M4/M5 should work without it.

findings.label: Brightness and the condition for it
findings.value: 300 nits per added screen; full brightness needs a power adapter plugged into one of the Trio's USB-C ports (passes through up to 65 W)
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Trio 3 Pro review (Simon Jary, Macworld, 2026-04-02)
findings.note: Macworld: without an adapter the Trio runs off the laptop's power. Macworld compares the 300 nits with the MacBook's 500-nit SDR peak. This is a stated figure, not a measurement.

findings.label: Weight on the lid (one added screen)
findings.value: 0.8 kg (1.8 lb), all of it held on the back of the lid by magnets
findings.source_title: Hands-on review: Mobile Pixels Duex Max DS (Owen McCarthy, FutureFive, 2024-02-19)
findings.note: FutureFive lists 'Weight 1.8 lbs (0.8kg)' and 'Plug and play via 2 USB-C port', with 300 nits adjustable. The magnets go on the back of the lid using the maker's template. McCarthy says the MacBook Pro's stiff lid reduced wobble; he does not discuss other laptops.

findings.label: Weight and video path (one stacked screen)
findings.value: About 1.3 kg; stands on its own kickstand (lid magnets optional); one USB-C cable, no driver on Windows or macOS; HDMI fallback needs separate power
findings.source_title: Mobile Pixels Duex Float 2 Pro Review (James Smythe, Mighty Gadget, 2026-08-16, updated 2026-08-20)
findings.note: Smythe: either USB-C port carries video, data and up to 65 W pass-through. Mini HDMI is the fallback for laptops without USB-C DisplayPort Alt Mode (cable not included). 350 nits is the stated spec, not measured. The review does not say how the weight splits between lid and table.

findings.label: Dual portable monitor (freestanding): weight and macOS limit
findings.value: 2.6 lb (about 1.18 kg) for two 14-inch 1920x1200 screens, about 0.59 kg per screen, nothing on the lid; dual-screen Extend not available on macOS (only the lower screen works when extending)
findings.source_title: Complete Guide to Dual-Screen Portable Monitors | ViewSonic
findings.note: This is a cited rival page; I include it so the table has a freestanding row. Its no-driver USB-C connection uses MST, which macOS does not support over USB-C. 65 W two-way USB-C PD. The kg conversion and per-screen division are my arithmetic. No brightness figure is given.
